The third arithmetic: queues, and why most lead time is waiting

Little's Law states that for a stable system, average work in progress equals average throughput multiplied by average cycle time. Rearranged, cycle time equals WIP divided by throughput. Titli's checkout squad in March had nine items in flight and completed an average of 1.5 items a week, giving a cycle time of 9 ÷ 1.5 = 6 weeks. Cutting WIP to four items, with throughput unchanged, gives 4 ÷ 1.5 = 2.7 weeks — a fifty-five per cent reduction in lead time from a decision that costs nothing and adds no people. Throughput typically improves as well, because context-switching falls, which makes the gain larger than the arithmetic predicts.

The companion measure is flow efficiency: the proportion of elapsed lead time during which anyone is actually touching the work. Titli measured 3.1 days of touch time against 19 working days of lead time on its median checkout item — sixteen per cent. Most teams that measure honestly land between five and fifteen per cent. The implication reframes the entire improvement conversation: a team obsessing over how fast it can code is optimising the sixteen per cent, while the eighty-four per cent sits in queues — waiting for a design decision, waiting for review, waiting for a test environment, waiting for a release window. Almost every large lifecycle improvement in practice is the removal of a queue, not an increase in effort.

4. When the model applies, and when it actively misleads

Three claims make the lifecycle useful, and each is testable rather than doctrinal. Apply them to both protagonists.

Claim one: the five transitions occur whether or not you name them. This is the claim that holds most nearly universally. Even a one-line hotfix passes through someone deciding it matters, deciding what the fix should be, writing it, convincing themselves it works, and releasing it. At Titli the transitions are compressed into hours and often into one person's head; at Pratibimb they occupy separate departments. The test is diagnostic: if you cannot say who performed a transition for a given change, it was performed implicitly, and implicit qualification is where escapes come from. Titli fails this test on its checkout work — nobody can say who validated the refund ledger design, because in Titli's culture design has no named moment.

Claim two: the cost of front-loading a decision should be compared to its expected reversal cost. This holds where you can estimate both terms. It fails where reversal cost is unbounded or unknowable — a regulatory breach, a data loss, a safety event — because there the expectation calculation is dominated by a tail you cannot price. That is why regulated industries use mandatory gates rather than economics: not because gates are efficient, but because expected-value reasoning is the wrong tool for ruin risks. Seven of Devika's sixty-one decisions sit in the tail region; fifty-four do not.

Claim three: batch size is the primary lever on lead time. This holds where the per-release fixed cost is small or reducible. It is actively misleading where the fixed cost is external. If Pratibimb halved its batch size while its customers' change-advisory boards still met monthly and their branch staff still needed a training cycle per release, lead time would not improve; work would simply queue outside Pratibimb's walls where Rohit cannot see it. The general warning: the lifecycle model misleads whenever the binding constraint sits outside the organisation drawing the diagram. Teams routinely optimise their own five transitions to beautiful effect and change nothing a customer can perceive.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Multi-product and platform organisations. When one team builds a platform that other teams consume, the platform's ship transition is the consumer team's envision transition, and the two lifecycles interlock at a seam nobody owns. The textbook answer is versioned interfaces and deprecation policy. What mature companies actually do is run the platform's new version alongside the old for a defined window — typically two to four quarters — and accept the carrying cost of two code paths, because forcing simultaneous migration means the platform team's qualification now includes every consumer's behaviour, which is unbounded. Pratibimb discovered this when it tried to change the shape of its loan-account identifier: eleven of its forty customers had built downstream reports against it, converting an internal design decision into a forty-party negotiation.

Two-sided markets. You cannot qualify one side in isolation. A change to how merchants see settlement alters what buyers experience at checkout, and a percentage rollout that touches only one side contaminates the measurement of the other. Marketplaces therefore qualify by market rather than by cohort — one city, one category, both sides at once — which converts the ship gate from a technical decision into a market-entry decision with commercial, supply and support preconditions. Titli's checkout will hit this: a refund policy that is correct for buyers and punishing for merchants will show up as improved buyer conversion and quiet merchant attrition, and no single-sided experiment will reveal it.

Regulated products. In lending, insurance and health, qualification's output is evidence, and the evidence is itself a deliverable. Pratibimb's customers must show their auditors that a change to an interest-computation routine was specified, approved, tested and released under change control, with the artefacts retained. The Reserve Bank of India's directions on digital lending, and customers' own internal audit functions, make the paper trail part of the product. The naive reading is that this forbids frequent releases. What sophisticated regulated companies do is separate the evidence from the ceremony: they generate traceability automatically from the pipeline — requirement identifier in the ticket, ticket identifier in the commit, commit in the test run, test run in the release record — so that producing an audit pack costs minutes rather than the nine person-days in Rohit's table. Compliance is not the enemy of frequency; manual evidence production is.

Hardware plus software. Here irreversibility is physical. The hardware lifecycle runs through its own gates — engineering validation, design validation, production validation — and after the production validation gate the injection-mould tooling has been cut and the bill of materials is frozen. Software attached to that hardware inherits a ship date it does not control and loses the option to decide late. Mature hardware companies handle this by making the shipped firmware as thin as possible — a bootloader and an over-the-air update channel — so that the irreversible artefact is the capability to update rather than the behaviour itself. Companies that skip this step discover, as the third worked example below shows, that a software defect has become a logistics problem.

AI-native products. A model-backed feature breaks the qualify transition in a specific way: there is no pass or fail, only a distribution. Qualification becomes an evaluation suite reporting that the system was acceptable on 91.4 per cent of a held-out set, and the product decision is what to do about the other 8.6 per cent — which is a question about the cost of a wrong answer to a user, not a question about the model. Two further complications are structural. First, the develop transition includes data and prompt changes that leave no trace in the code repository unless someone deliberately versions them, so the "what changed?" question that every incident begins with may have no answer. Second, if the model is a third-party API, a vendor can change behaviour on their schedule, which means qualification must be continuous rather than per-release. Pratyaksh Systems, a Hyderabad company building document-extraction software for insurers, learned this when a vendor model upgrade moved its field-extraction accuracy from 94 per cent to 89 per cent overnight with no change on its side; it now runs its evaluation suite nightly against a frozen sample of 1,200 documents and treats a two-point drop as a production incident.

6. Ten distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A phase is a property of a change, not of a calendar

The competent practitioner says "we are in the development phase this quarter." The expert hears that sentence as a confession that the team pushes one large batch through the transitions per quarter, and asks how many independent changes are in it. At any instant in a healthy team, different changes occupy all five states simultaneously. The tell in the wild is a status report organised by phase rather than by change; the obvious reading — that the team is disciplined — is wrong, because what the report actually reveals is maximal batch size and therefore maximal blast radius.

Deployment, release and launch are three separable events

Code reaching a server, behaviour reaching a user, and a message reaching the market are distinct, and every one of them can be decoupled from the others. The tell is a team that says "we cannot ship until marketing is ready." That sentence means engineering cadence has been welded to the marketing calendar, which guarantees that qualification will be compressed whenever a campaign date moves — the single most reliable predictor of a bad release. Titli separates all three by default; Pratibimb conflates them, which is why a documentation delay becomes a code delay.

Qualification is evidence production, not defect hunting

A clean test report answers only whether the artefact matches the specification. It cannot tell you whether the specification was right, because the tests were derived from it. The expert reads an exit report looking for three separate warrants: verification (does it match the spec), validation (does it solve the problem — a judgement only the product manager can make), and operability (rollback path, monitoring, support runbook, the ability of a support agent to explain the change). The tell is a release gate whose only metric is open-defect count.

The product manager's authority curve is not a presence curve

Decision authority is high at envision, falls through design, is near zero through develop, and rises again at qualify and ship. Availability runs the other way: during develop the PM is consulted constantly and must answer fast, in writing, without deciding things that are not hers. The tell of a misread is a PM who attends every stand-up while design decisions still queue behind her. The obvious reading is that she is engaged; the correct reading is that she has made herself a dependency in the one transition where her judgement adds least and her latency costs most.

The what/how boundary does not sit where the slogan puts it

"Product owns what, engineering owns how" collapses at the data model and the interface contract. Whether an approval threshold is a constant, a per-tenant setting or a contract attribute; whether an identifier is stable across a merge; whether an operation is idempotent; what the system promises when it is half-broken — these are commitments to customers expressed in schemas. The tell is a product manager who has never read an API contract. The cost arrives two years later, when a routine customer request turns out to require a migration, and everyone calls it technical debt rather than an unexamined product decision.

The cost-of-change curve is real, but its slope is a purchase

Practitioners quote 1:10:100 as physics. It is an empirical observation about particular projects in particular decades, and Table 2 shows a single team with two slopes at once. The expert's move is to ask what the organisation's actual right-hand value is — how long until a bad change is noticed, how many users it touches, how long to undo — and to treat those three numbers as levers. The tell is an argument about process discipline in which nobody has cited the mean time to detect a production defect.

Rollback is not recovery

Reverting code is easy; reverting data is often impossible. A change that adds a column, backfills it and starts writing to it has a straightforward code rollback and a one-way data path. The expert reads any rollback plan by asking what happens to the records written while the new behaviour was live. The tell is a release checklist with a rollback line and no data line. This is also why "everything is reversible if you have flags" is false: flags reverse behaviour, not consequences, and the consequences are what customers experienced.

Estimates degrade in a predictable, asymmetric way

The cone of uncertainty, as Boehm framed it and Steve McConnell popularised it, holds that estimates made at concept are accurate within roughly a factor of four and tighten to about 1.25× by detailed design. The expert treats the cone as a warning rather than a promise: Todd Little's 2006 study of several hundred projects found that in practice the cone often does not narrow, because new uncertainty enters as fast as old uncertainty resolves. The practical consequence is that an estimate given at envision should be quoted as a range with a date attached to the range, and re-quoted at the design gate; the tell of a novice is a single number carried unchanged from kickoff to commitment.

Discovery is a parallel activity, not an antecedent phase

Customer interviews, instrumentation analysis and prototypes run continuously at their own cadence and supply the evidence that envision consumes. The tell is a team whose research stops the moment building starts — precisely when the sharpest questions appear, because building forces specificity that conversation allows people to avoid. Cagan's dual-track formulation names this; the common misreading turns dual-track into two sequential tracks with a handover, which is the original problem wearing a new label.

The lifecycle hides a queue, and the queue is most of the elapsed time

When flow efficiency is sixteen per cent, the difference between a fast team and a slow one is almost entirely in the waiting, not the working. The expert's first diagnostic on a slow team is not "are the engineers productive" but "where does work sit still, and who is it waiting for" — usually a shared environment, a single reviewer, an approval board, or a product manager's inbox. The tell is a team that responds to a speed complaint by proposing to work longer hours.

7. How this differs across product types and company stages

Say plainly where the differences are real and where they are not. The five transitions themselves do not vary; what varies is the cost of exposure, which determines where qualification happens. In consumer products, exposure is cheap and statistically informative: Titli can route one per cent of eleven million users to a change and read a significant result on conversion within a day. Qualification therefore migrates into production, where it is called experimentation, and front-loading is light. In B2B and enterprise software, exposure is expensive and statistically useless: forty customers do not make an experiment, and a change to a screen generates support calls and retraining whether or not it is an improvement. Qualification must therefore precede exposure, in staging environments and customer acceptance testing, and the ship gate becomes a negotiated event with release notes, windows and sometimes contractual notice periods.

Platforms and marketplaces differ structurally rather than in degree, as section 5 described: platforms have a seam where one team's ship is another's envision, and marketplaces cannot qualify one side alone. Hardware products face genuine irreversibility at the tooling gate, which is the only context in this topic where "decide late" is simply unavailable. AI products change the nature of qualification from binary to distributional, and make the develop transition include artefacts — data, prompts, model versions — that traditional version control does not capture unless someone insists.

Where the difference is not real is worth stating too. The distinction between consumer and enterprise does not change who holds the envision and ship gates; a product manager owns both in either setting. It does not change the value of separating deployment from release; Pratibimb can deploy code to customer environments dormant behind configuration long before any customer sees it, and several of its competitors do. And it does not change the queue arithmetic: an enterprise team with a nine-item work-in-progress limit is slow for exactly the same reason a consumer team is.

Stage changes the failure mode rather than the model. In a twelve-person startup the five transitions collapse into conversations and the founder holds all the gates without noticing; the characteristic failure is that qualification is skipped entirely and nobody detects the difference until the first customer with real volume arrives. At around a hundred and fifty people — where Pratibimb was six years ago — each transition acquires an owner, a form and a meeting, and the failure inverts: gates become rituals nobody can fail, and the real decisions migrate into code because the official channel is too slow. At a thousand people the dominant cost is the seams between lifecycles, not any lifecycle itself, and the leverage moves from process design to interface design.

The structural fix was not more testing. Vritti redefined what the irreversible artefact was: the next product shipped with a minimal bootloader and an update channel sized and paid for as a first-class requirement, so that the hardware gate froze the capability to change rather than the behaviour itself. Its first field update after that was a 220 KB delta delivered in four days. The lifecycle lesson generalises beyond hardware: when a ship gate is genuinely irreversible, the highest leverage move is not to qualify harder before it but to redesign what passes through it.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings, and the cost of catching them late

Qualification compression. The early warning is a planned-versus-actual test window that shrinks release after release while nobody records the decision. The diagnostic question is not "did we test enough" but "what specifically did we not test, and what class of defect would it have caught" — a question that forces the dropped scope into words. Vritti could have answered it in one sentence on 20 July. Caught at the gate, the cost was a fortnight of schedule; caught in the field, ₹1.9 crore and seven months.

The silent design decision. An engineer encounters an ambiguity the specification did not resolve and resolves it sensibly in code. The early warning is acceptance criteria containing "TBD" or a defined term that appears nowhere in a glossary. The diagnostic question, asked in any backlog refinement: "which item in this sprint contains a decision nobody outside this room has seen?" Caught then, it costs a five-minute conversation; caught in production it costs an incident, and the organisational damage is worse than the money because the engineer is usually blamed for a failure of specification.

The product manager as a queue. The early warning is a rising count of items blocked on "waiting for product" combined with a PM whose calendar is full of squad ceremonies. The diagnostic is to ask two engineers to name the last three decisions the squad made without the PM; if they cannot, she is the constraint. The cost of catching it late is measured in flow efficiency — at sixteen per cent, a two-day product response time on each of three touchpoints is most of the lead time.

The invisible ship gate. Nobody can name the person who says no. The early warning is a release that happens on a date rather than on a condition. The diagnostic question is "who declined a release in the last six months, and on what grounds?" — if the answer is nobody, the gate is decorative. The late cost is that when a bad release does occur, the organisation discovers it had no decision to review and therefore learns nothing.

The big-bang re-platform. The lifecycle traversed exactly once at maximum batch size, typically over eighteen months, with qualification concentrated at the end. The early warning is a plan whose first customer-visible value arrives after month nine. The diagnostic question is "what does a user get in month three?" The late cost is the familiar one: a cutover whose risk cannot be decomposed, and a rollback path that exists on paper only.

Discovery debt. Work enters envision on the strength of a single customer sentence relayed by a sales conversation. The early warning is a roadmap item whose written rationale names a customer but no behaviour and no number. The diagnostic question is "what evidence would change our mind about this?" — if none exists, the item is a request, not a problem. The late cost is a shipped feature with no adoption, which is the most expensive possible outcome because it consumed the full lifecycle and produced nothing to learn from.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether the cost-of-change curve is steep by nature. The Boehm position holds that defects grow more expensive the later they are found, and that this justifies serious up-front specification. The counter-position, argued most sharply by Laurent Bossavit in The Leprechauns of Software Engineering (2012), is that the famous curve rests on a thin and frequently miscited evidence base, and that Kent Beck's claim of a flattened curve under modern practice has never been decisively refuted either. Steelmanned, Boehm's side says: architectural and data-model errors genuinely do compound, and no amount of tooling makes a wrong schema cheap after three years of writes. Steelmanned, Beck's side says: for the overwhelming majority of changes, the curve has been flattened by automated tests, flags and fast rollback, and citing 1981 economics to justify 2026 process is an appeal to authority. What would settle it is per-organisation measurement of the kind in Table 2 — which almost nobody does, which is why the argument persists.

Whether the DORA findings establish causation. The Accelerate research reports that elite performers deploy more frequently and fail less often, and infers that small batches cause stability. The strongest objection is methodological: the data is survey-based, self-reported, cross-sectional, and heavily weighted toward web-delivered software. Elite performers may deploy often because their systems are well-architected rather than the reverse, and the sampling frame contains very little firmware, embedded or regulated batch-release work. Steelmanned, the defenders point to the mechanism — small changes are attributable, and attributable failures are fast to fix — which is independent of the survey. For the position to be wrong, you would need a context where failure detection does not improve with smaller batches; Vritti's forty-day latent defect is precisely such a context, and it is why the finding should be applied to firmware with care.

Whether a product manager belongs inside the develop transition at all. One school, associated with Marty Cagan's empowered product teams, holds that product, design and engineering sit together continuously and that separating discovery from delivery re-creates the handover it was meant to remove; on this view a PM who withdraws from daily contact is abdicating. The opposing school holds that continuous presence creates decision dependency, slows the team and blurs accountability, and that the PM's leverage is concentrated at two boundaries. Steelmanned, the first rests on the observation that most product failures come from insufficient shared context; the second rests on the observation that most delivery failures come from waiting. They may simply describe different constraints: the first is right when the team lacks context, the second when the team lacks autonomy. The honest position is that neither has evidence beyond practitioner testimony.

Whether estimation is worth doing. The #NoEstimates argument, associated with Woody Zuill and Vasco Duarte, holds that estimates consume effort, are systematically wrong, and are used as commitments regardless of how they were framed; slice work small and count throughput instead. The forecasting school, associated with Troy Magennis and with Monte Carlo methods over historical throughput, agrees that single-point estimates are indefensible but argues that a probability distribution over completion dates is both achievable and necessary, because organisations must coordinate with marketing, sales and regulators. For #NoEstimates to be wrong, it would have to be true that small consistent slices are unavailable in your context — which is often the case in regulated or hardware work. For forecasting to be wrong, throughput would have to be non-stationary enough that history carries no signal, which is common in early-stage teams.

Whether regulated qualification can be continuous. The compliance-as-code position holds that the auditor wants evidence, evidence can be generated automatically, and there is no regulation that mandates a quarterly cadence. The opposing position holds that audit in practice is a human process in which a named person attests, that customers' own change-advisory boards are real organisational facts outside the vendor's control, and that a vendor who ships monthly into a customer that can absorb quarterly has simply moved the queue. Rohit sits precisely on this fault line, and his table shows both sides are partly right: automation removed fifty-five of ninety-three fixed days, and could not touch the twenty-four that belong to his customer.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the lifecycle can name the five transitions and argue about agile. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways. First, they classify before they process: presented with a body of work, their first act is to sort decisions by reversal cost rather than by size or by theme, and only the irreversible subset gets ceremony. Second, they treat the release architecture as a product decision they are accountable for: they know their team's mean time to detect a production defect, and they treat improving it as work that competes with features, because it is what buys the right to decide late. Third, they hold two gates hard and stay out of the middle: an envision memo that names the problem, the terms that must not be interpreted in code, and what would count as success; and a ship gate with a named person, a stated exposure sequence, and a condition for stopping. Fourth, they read queues rather than effort: when told a team is slow, they ask where work sits still, and they are unsurprised when the answer turns out to be their own inbox.

The negative signal is equally recognisable. Masters do not argue about methodology names. They ask what the batch size is, what a mistake costs, how fast anyone would know, and who says no. Those four questions do more work than any framework, and they are answerable in any company on any Tuesday.

12. What each protagonist decided

Devika took the middle row of Table 4. On 19 March she published a two-page classification of the sixty-one checkout decisions, with the seven irreversible ones named, each assigned an owner, a written design and a review that included Titli's finance controller and external counsel. The other fifty-four went through Titli's normal machinery untouched. She added one permanent change: a standing question in the team's change template asking what it would cost to undo this and how quickly we would know, which routes a change into the heavy path only when it earns it. Her reasoning was that the danger was never the payments work; it was the precedent that high stakes justify heavy process everywhere, which would have cost the company its nineteen-hour lead time to protect seven decisions.

Rohit did not commit to monthly. On 24 March he proposed a six-weekly cadence from the first quarter of the new financial year, funded by a ₹43.4 lakh automation programme, with monthly releases offered contractually from the following year conditional on the customer accepting a two-week UAT window for releases under twenty changes. His reasoning was that the fixed cost of qualification, not the cadence, was the thing he was actually negotiating, and that promising monthly before the fixed cost fell would have forced the compression that produced Vritti's ₹1.9 crore. He sent the customer the table.

Three questions in the manner of a teaching note. First: Devika's classification rests on her team's own estimate of reversal cost, and the seven irreversible decisions were identified by the people who would be most inconvenienced by calling something irreversible — what mechanism, if any, should check that judgement, and what does it cost? Second: Rohit's automation case assumes 232 changes a year remains constant, but shorter cycles usually increase demand for changes because customers see that asking is worthwhile — if volume rises to 340, does his argument survive, and which row of Table 3 breaks first? Third: both protagonists treat the product manager's authority as concentrated at the envision and ship gates, yet the defect that cost Vritti ₹1.9 crore was created by a procurement decision about a data tariff that no product manager saw — where, in the five transitions, should that decision have surfaced, and who should have been accountable for noticing that it had not?

13. Going deeper

The immediate neighbour is Waterfall, Agile and Lean, which supplies the vocabulary for the batch-size argument this page has made implicitly and explains why three schools that appear to disagree about phases are really disagreeing about queue length. Agile in practice turns that argument into weekly mechanics and is worth reading with the caution that the mechanics are not the point; teams that master the ceremonies and never shrink their batch have bought the costume. Kanban and flow is the direct continuation of the third arithmetic in section 3 — work in progress limits, Little's Law and flow efficiency — and is the fastest available source of lead-time improvement in most organisations. The execution rhythm addresses the layer above: how planning, review and escalation cycles interlock so that the gates in this page have somewhere to happen.

On the estimation and scoping side, Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing takes up the cone-of-uncertainty problem and the disagreement in section 10, and matters because most lifecycle arguments are proxies for a disagreement about commitment. Backlog management and refinement is where the silent design decision is caught or missed, and is therefore the cheapest place to prevent the second failure mode in section 9. Definition of done sharpens the qualify transition into something a team can actually exit, and is the antidote to gates that nobody can fail. The PM–engineering relationship is the human layer beneath the authority curve, and is what determines whether a product manager who withdraws from stand-ups is read as trusting or as absent.

Two topics extend the argument into harder terrain. Technical debt: rewrite or build on is the other face of reversal cost — debt is precisely the accumulated expense of past decisions one would now like to unwind — and gives the language for deciding when the cheap-reversal architecture is worth rebuilding rather than patching. Hardware development cycles shows what the lifecycle looks like when a gate is genuinely irreversible because tooling has been cut, and is the context in which Vritti's mistake stops being avoidable by diligence and becomes a question of what you allow to pass through the gate at all.
